## Why this design — theoretical framework

The references below ground the module's pedagogical design (see
[teaching-design.qmd](teaching-design.qmd) and [ai-tutor.qmd](ai-tutor.qmd)). They are given
to help you situate the course; none needs to be read fully to succeed, but each can inform
a part of your reflexive report.

- **Co-constructed learning**: knowledge is built in interaction
  [@vygotsky1978mind], and students take part in designing their own track
  [@bovill2011co_creators; @cook_sather2014partners; @aldinhe2023co_constructing], in the
  tradition of critical pedagogy [@freire1970pedagogy].
- **Learning contracts**: how to write objectives, sequencing and success criteria — the
  Waterloo Centre for Teaching Excellence factsheet
  [@waterloo2023learning_contracts].
- **Learning by teaching with AI**: teaching an agent structures learning
  [@schmucker2024ruffle]; conversational tutoring best practices preserve the student's
  agency and integrate knowledge tracing [@arxiv2026path_conversational]; a randomized
  trial (N=194) suggests that well-designed AI tutoring can outperform active learning in
  class [@nature2025ai_tutoring_rct] — a result to be confirmed.
- **Dialogue and reflexivity**: dialogic pedagogy applied to LLMs [@beale2025dialogic].

## Documented limits of AI in education

The module treats these limits as objects of work, not taboos:

- Hallucinations and reinforcement of misconceptions [@mdpi2025chatbots_challenges].
- Over-reliance and risk of losing basic skills [@kasneci2023chatgpt]; cognitive
  offloading and "cognitive debt" [@risko2016cognitive_offloading;
  @kosmyna2025brain_chatgpt]; instrumental trust in an assistant [@cao2022reliance].
- Often superficial student uses [@stohr2024chatbots_beliefs] and adoption conditioned by
  trust and institutional policy [@taylor2024chatgpt_adoption; @springer2025reimagining_he].
- Resistance, access inequalities and postures toward technology [@selwyn2019robots;
  @frontiers2025mitigating_resistance]; student viewpoints
  [@arxiv2025student_perspectives]; state of the art of pedagogical agents
  [@springer2025pedagogical_agents].
- For those interested in technique as *individuation* and not merely a tool:
  [@simondon1964individuation].

## Official technical resources

The primary reference for the technique remains the official documentation — your tutor
(Track A) and your own research (Track B) must always be checkable against it.

- Asynchronous Python: [`asyncio`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html)
  [@python_asyncio].
- Multiprocess and IPC: [`multiprocessing`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html)
  [@python_multiprocessing].
- Distributed computing: [Dask delayed](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/delayed.html)
  [@dask_docs] and [Ray](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/) [@ray_docs].
- Vectorization: [numpy ufunc](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/ufuncs.html)
  [@numpy_ufunc] and [numba](https://numba.readthedocs.io/) [@numba_docs].
- GPU: [CuPy](https://docs.cupy.dev/) [@cupy_docs] and
  [numba CUDA](https://numba.readthedocs.io/en/stable/cuda/index.html) [@numba_docs].
- WebGPU: [WebGPU specification](https://gpuweb.github.io/gpuweb/) [@webgpu_spec] and the
  [WGSL language](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/) [@wgsl_spec].
